analysis.one_liner: Shields employers from federal orders over plant closings and lets them warn of union costs without penalty.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 35 Republican cosponsors but never got a vote, dying in a House subcommittee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act so that when employers tell workers that unions, bargaining, or strikes raise costs, those statements cannot be used as evidence of unlawful anti-union motive, as long as they contain no threats or promises of benefit. It would also strip the National Labor Relations Board of power to order a company to restore, move back, or keep a facility, or to block future moves, unless a court has finally ruled the company acted unlawfully — for example, by closing or moving work without notice or directly to punish organizing. In practice, it would remove the Board's main tools against plant closings and relocations aimed at union activity.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies deciding where to build, move, or close plants — especially those shifting work out of unionized states into right-to-work states — would gain near-immunity from Board orders to restore moved or eliminated work, and could tell employees that unions raise costs without those statements counting against them. The setting that prompted the bill was the National Labor Relations Board's 2011 complaint over Boeing's new 787 production line in South Carolina, a right-to-work state, which business groups called punishment of a lawful location decision.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers weighing closures, moves, or anti-union campaigns

how_it_helps.text: Employer statements about the costs of collective bargaining, work stoppages, or strikes could not constitute or be evidence of antiunion animus or unlawful motive, so long as they contain no threat of reprisal or force or promise of benefit.

The National Labor Relations Board would lose power to order an employer to relocate, shut down, or transfer work, or to prevent future moves or closures, unless the employer had been finally adjudicated in court to have acted unlawfully — either without advance notice to the union of the economic reasons, or as a primary and direct response to organizing.

Nothing in the Act could prevent an employer from choosing where to locate, develop, or expand its business, close facilities, or eliminate jobs, absent such a final court adjudication; the bill's title frames this as clarifying the law's application to right-to-work states.

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to organize, union members in labor disputes, and communities near plants on the chopping block: a closure or relocation aimed at punishing organizing could stand for years while any case worked its way to a final ruling, by which time the jobs are gone, and employer warnings that unions cost jobs could no longer be weighed as evidence of illegal motive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers organizing unions or facing plant closures

drawbacks.text: Retaliatory closings would be nearly impossible to remedy: the Board could not act against a closure or relocation until a court had finally adjudicated the employer's action unlawful, a process that takes years, during which the affected jobs have already disappeared.

Employer messaging that unions or strikes raise costs could no longer be used as evidence of unlawful motive even during an organizing drive, making retaliation cases harder for the Board to prove from circumstantial patterns.

The shield protects even first-time violators: only an employer already finally adjudicated to have acted unlawfully loses the bill's protections, so a company could punish organizing once and face no closure-related remedy for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters' case: no federal board should dictate where a company builds a plant, and the Board's complaint over Boeing's South Carolina 787 line looked to critics like punishing a legal business decision; the speech provision largely restates the idea that employers may discuss unionization without threats or promises of benefit. The cost falls on the enforcement side: it removes the practical deterrent against closing or moving work to punish union activity, since remedies would wait on a final court ruling while jobs vanish, and cost-of-union messaging could no longer serve as evidence of motive. The scales tip clearly toward employers, and that is how the bill lined up in practice — every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2011 and sent to the House education committee and then a subcommittee, it never received a hearing vote or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Scott of South Carolina introduced the bill on May 24, 2011, joined at introduction by four South Carolina Republican colleagues: Joe Wilson, Trey Gowdy, Jeff Duncan, and Mick Mulvaney.
The House referred it the same day to the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On September 8, 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — the last recorded action on the bill.
It drew 35 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never received a committee or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers kept the existing National Labor Relations Act remedies the bill would have stripped, including Board power over retaliatory closings; employers lost nothing they do not already have, since the law stayed exactly as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, who kept existing labor-law remedies

for.name: Rep. Tim Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Job Protection Act on May 24, 2011, framed as clarifying the labor law's application to right-to-work states like South Carolina.

for.name: Reps. Joe Wilson, Trey Gowdy, Jeff Duncan, and Mick Mulvaney
for.what_they_did: Joined Scott as original cosponsors at the bill's introduction.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote; it sat in the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor, the four South Carolina colleagues who joined him at introduction, and all 35 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Republican-run committee never scheduled a vote [S3][S4][S5].

industries.industry: Multi-site employers weighing closures or relocations, especially manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would bar the labor board from ordering work restored or blocking moves and closures, and would shield employer statements about union costs from use as evidence of unlawful motive. Sponsors framed it around right-to-work states; the immediate backdrop was the Board's case over Boeing's new 787 line in South Carolina. The gain comes at the expense of workers' leverage and remedies.

industries.industry: Labor unions and workers seeking to organize
industries.note: The bill would remove the board's power to order relocated or eliminated work restored except after a final court ruling, and would stop employer cost-of-union messaging from counting as evidence of antiunion motive. Both changes would weaken unions' chief tools against closure and relocation retaliation.
